difficultyRationale: A subtle but common production pitfall: coordinating timeouts across hops, not just setting one on each call in isolation.
prompt: Service A has a 5-second overall deadline for a user request and makes a call to B with that same 5-second deadline. B invokes C with another independently configured 5-second timeout even though part of A's deadline has already elapsed. A correctly times out at its own 5-second deadline, but B and C may continue working after A has given up. What is the timeout-budget design error?
explanation: A properly enforced five-second deadline at A does not become ten seconds merely because B separately configures a five-second C timeout. Instead, if B gives C a fresh five seconds after some of A's budget is gone, B/C may still work after A has timed out. Propagate remaining deadlines and cancellation or choose shorter child timeouts that fit inside the caller's remaining budget.

options.text: Each downstream timeout should be bounded by the caller's remaining deadline (minus processing/transport margin); giving C an independent fresh 5-second timeout after A's budget has partly elapsed wastes work after A has already timed out, unless deadline/cancellation is propagated.
options.explanation: Correct. A should not wait ten seconds if its configured total timeout is five; the actual harm is that B/C may outlive A's deadline, consume resources uselessly, and fail to return useful work. Propagate an absolute deadline or remaining budget.

options.text: Because A and B both configured a five-second timeout, A itself is guaranteed to take ten seconds to return a timeout to its client even if A correctly enforces its five-second overall deadline.
options.explanation: An enforced overall deadline of five seconds prevents A from waiting ten seconds. The real issue is unnecessary downstream work that continues beyond that deadline.

options.text: Timeouts only apply to the network transport layer, not to how long a service spends processing after a call returns, so B's 5-second timeout on C has no bearing on how long A ultimately waits — the delay must come from A's own processing instead.
options.explanation: A downstream call contributes to end-to-end latency, and deadline propagation is essential to prevent wasted processing and resource exhaustion after callers have timed out.

options.text: The fix is to remove B's timeout on its call to C entirely, since B should always wait as long as it takes for C to answer rather than fail early — removing the inner timeout eliminates the compounding delay seen at A.
options.explanation: Removing the downstream timeout can leave B waiting on C indefinitely and does not enforce A's deadline. The child call should be bounded by remaining budget.

references.title: Google Site Reliability Engineering book — Addressing Cascading Failures (deadline/timeout propagation across a call chain)
